question: Can pretraining an LSTM on unlabeled sequences (language model or sequence autoencoder) stabilise and improve later supervised LSTM text classification?
hypothesis: The sequence autoencoder can memorise the input and gives gradient shortcuts, so it is a good, stable initialisation for recurrent networks; more unlabeled data should improve generalisation.
contributions: Two unsupervised pretraining methods for LSTMs: recurrent language model (LM-LSTM) and sequence autoencoder (SA-LSTM)
Pretraining makes LSTMs trainable on documents of a few hundred timesteps and matches or beats previous best on IMDB, Rotten Tomatoes, 20 Newsgroups, DBpedia
More unlabeled data from a related domain improves the supervised model

method.summary: An LSTM is pretrained either as a next-step language model or as a sequence autoencoder (encoder and decoder share weights; reads the whole document then reproduces it), then its embeddings and LSTM weights initialise a supervised classifier that reads the label from the last timestep and is fine-tuned end to end with early stopping.
method.task: unsupervised pretraining then supervised document classification (sentiment, topic) and CIFAR-10 row-wise image classification

datasets.name: IMDB (Maas et al. 2011)
datasets.size: 25,000 labeled + 50,000 unlabeled train, 25,000 test; mean 241 words, max 2,526
datasets.preprocessing: punctuation as separate tokens; words appearing once in the dataset removed; no weighting or stemming

datasets.name: Amazon movie reviews (McAuley and Leskovec 2013)
datasets.size: 7.9 million movie reviews used (of 34 million product reviews)

datasets.name: 20 Newsgroups (Lang 1995)
datasets.preprocessing: attachments, PGP keys, duplicates and empty messages removed

datasets.name: DBpedia (Lehmann et al. 2014; Zhang and LeCun 2015 split)
datasets.size: 560,000 train, 70,000 test, 14 classes; mean 300 characters, max 13,467
datasets.preprocessing: character-level input; non-English characters and words ignored

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.preprocessing: data augmentation as in Krizhevsky et al. 2012; each timestep is one row of pixels

models.name: SA-LSTM / LM-LSTM
models.architecture: LSTM RNN with input, forget, output gates; word (or character) embeddings
models.init_from: unsupervised sequence autoencoder or recurrent language model
models.layers: 1 (IMDB, inferred: no other count given); 2 for DBpedia (3 in best variant); 1 or 2 for CIFAR-10
models.hidden: 1,024 memory cells, 512-unit input embedding, 512-unit hidden layer with 50% dropout before the classifier (30 units in later experiments); DBpedia 512 per layer, embedding 128; CIFAR-10 400 units
models.context: full document, backprop truncated to 400 timesteps from the end

other.hidden layer note: IMDB tuned plain LSTM used 512 hidden units

models.name: LSTM with word2vec embeddings
models.init_from: word2vec embeddings (Google News or trained on Amazon reviews)

training.objective: pretrain: next-step prediction (LM) or reconstruct the input after an end-of-sentence marker (autoencoder, shared encoder/decoder weights); CIFAR-10 uses Euclidean L2 distance between predicted and target row. Supervised: classification from last-timestep LSTM output; variants linear label gain (label at every step, weights rising 0 to 1) and joint training with the autoencoder
training.dropout: chosen on validation: IMDB 80% input embedding dims; Rotten Tomatoes 95% embedding + 50% word; 20NG 70% embedding + 75% word; DBpedia none; 50% on hidden layer before classifier
training.regularisation: embedding-dimension dropout, random word dropout, early stopping when validation error rises, clipping of cell outputs and gradients (Sutskever et al. recipe)
training.hardware: GPU (memory use mentioned, type not stated)

other.fine-tuning: both embeddings and LSTM weights fine-tuned

baselines: ConvNets (Kim 2014; Johnson and Zhang 2014; Zhang and LeCun 2015)
eval.protocol: single reported number per cell; no seeds, variance or significance tests stated; hyperparameters (dropout) chosen on validation set

limits: No optimizer, learning rate, schedule, GPU type, compute or seed information; single runs, no variance or significance
Hyperparameters tuned per dataset on validation sets; dropout rates differ widely across tasks
Text and Table 2 disagree on LM-LSTM IMDB error (8.98% vs 7.64%)
Rotten Tomatoes gain from Amazon data confounds domain match with data volume; no scaling curve over unlabeled data size
SA vs LM comparison is mixed: LM wins on 20NG, DBpedia (w/o gain) and CIFAR-10; authors' short-term-objective explanation is a hypothesis, not tested
Only supervised classification evaluated; LSTMs are dated vs transformers; CIFAR-10 below state-of-the-art convnets (authors concede)
Hypothesis about why the autoencoder works (memorisation, gradient shortcuts) is not tested
No code or weights released in the paper
